description_block:
FAITH RINGGOLD (1930-2024)
Seven Passages to a Flight 
signed and dated 'Faith Ringgold 9/15/98' (lower right)
hand-painted and hand-stenciled etchings and letterpress text on linen, pieced and quilted with patchwork borders accompanied by artist's book and printer's archive
quilt: 49 5/8 x 42 in (126 x 106.5 cm)
 book: 9 1/2 x 7 7/8 x 7/8 in (24 x 19.9 x 2 cm)
Executed 1995-98, this quilt is the publisher's copy set aside from an intended edition of 30, of which 15 were realized, and the book is number three from an edition of 30

Provenance
Bill Kelly Collection, San Diego (acquired directly from the artist).

Seven Passages to a Flight is among Faith Ringgold's deeply personal autobiographical works, 
bringing together image, text, printmaking and quilting in the distinctive narrative form for which she 
is celebrated. The present quilt incorporates the nine hand-painted and hand-stenciled etchings 
created for the artist's book, arranged with Ringgold's text and quilted in a diamond pattern that 
echoes the work's geometric borders. The composition is surrounded by a richly patterned 
patchwork border finished with two layers of piping. The printed limitation statement records an 
intended edition of thirty quilts, comprising ten numbered in Roman numerals and twenty lettered A
T. According to the records of Brighton Press, however, only 15 quilts were ultimately produced, 
making the present work exceptionally rare. Examples are held in the collections of the Museum of 
Modern Art, New York; The San Diego Museum of Art; and the Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art at 
Cornell University. 

The quilt is accompanied by the corresponding artist's book, Seven Passages to a Flight, published by 
Brighton Press in 1995. Its nine etchings were printed on linen and individually painted and stenciled 
by hand, while Ringgold's text was set in Perpetua and printed letterpress. The imagery created for 
the book is reproduced within the quilt, establishing the two works as closely related expressions of 
the same autobiographical narrative. The quilt is accompanied by the publisher's copy of the artist's 
book and a small archive assembled by Brighton Press co-founder and director Bill Kelly, himself a 
painter, printmaker and sculptor. The archive comprises six proofs of the hand-colored etchings 
printed on five sheets of linen (one double-sided): two black-and-white proofs in an early state; two 
colored proofs printed without borders, one with pencil outlines indicating the border; and two 
double-page spreads of text and etching within multicolored pochoir borders. Also included are the 
printer's mock-up of the binding boards and a single sheet bearing a quotation inscribed five times in 
Ringgold's hand: "My father said we tore up the pattern for that one F.R." Together, the artist's book 
and archive provide an unusually rich record of the conception and production of this rare story quilt.
material: hand-painted and hand-stenciled etchings and letterpress text on linen, pieced and quilted with patchwork borders
provenance: Bill Kelly Collection, San Diego (acquired directly from the artist).
subject_matter: quilt, etchings, letterpress text, patchwork, geometric patterns, colored images, autobiographical narrative, figures, border designs, artist's book

description_block:
PROPERTY FROM A SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA COLLECTIONANDY WARHOL (1928-1987)
Mark Leibovitz 
signed, inscribed and dated 'Mark L. Andy Warhol 1977' (on the overlap); inscribed 'Mark, with love Andy Warhol' (on the reverse)
acrylic and silkscreen ink on linen
40 x 40 in (101.6 x 101.6 cm)
Executed in 1977

Provenance
Mark Leibovitz Collection, New York (acquired directly from the artist).
Thence by descent to the present owner.

Literature
N. Printz & S. King-Nero, eds., The Andy Warhol Catalogue Raisonné: Paintings and Sculptures 1976-1978, Volume 5, New York, 2018, no. 3623 (illustrated p. 217).

By 1977, sitting for Andy Warhol had become a coveted status symbol in New York City. From celebrities to socialites and art world giants, the rich and famous aspired to be immortalized by Warhol, commissioning him for his now iconic portraits. Bursting with the energy of the decade, Mark Leibovitz, which Ian Schaffner places among Warhol's "signature portraits" (I. Schaffner, Essential Warhol, New York, 1999, p. 83), captures the essence of the year: in the spring of 1977, Studio 54 opened its doors to Manhattan's finest, and by December, Saturday Night Fever had sent disco around the globe. 

Born in Los Angeles on May 5, 1947, Mark Phillip Leibovitz studied at the University of California, Santa Barbara, before earning his J.D. from Hastings College of the Law in San Francisco (now UC Law San Francisco). Though trained as a lawyer, Mark gravitated toward the arts, and over the course of the 1970s opened several galleries in San Francisco. By the end of the decade, the young Leibovitz was catapulted into the vibrant Manhattan art scene, joining one of New York City's oldest art galleries, Knoedler, as a dealer. Ultimately, Mark found his true passion in real estate, staking an early claim on property in Hell's Kitchen and the Upper West Side. 

Through the late 1970s and 1980s, Mark became an active member of New York City's cultural and social circles, a familiar presence at Studio 54 and a friend to artists like Warhol and Salvador Dalí. Although his life was cut short in 1987, the same year as Warhol's, Mark Leibovitz stands as a testament to Mark's spirit, charisma and love for the arts during an unforgettable period in Manhattan's history. The present work, with its blurred contours and washes of saturated color, gives the portrait the quality of a half-remembered night, the sitter caught at the height of his youth in an era that was already becoming a legend.

description_block:
BANKSY (B. 1974)
Gangsta Rat (Mint) 
signed and numbered 'Banksy 3/8' (lower left)
screenprint in colors on wove paper
19 3/4 x 13 7/8 in (50 x 35.2 cm)
Executed in 2004, this work is number three from an edition of eight

This work is accompanied by a certificate of authenticity issued by Pest Control Office.

Provenance
Pictures On Walls Ltd., London.
Acquired from the above by the present owner in 2015.

Among the most instantly recognizable images in Banksy's celebrated oeuvre, Gangsta Rat distills the artist's irreverent wit and incisive social commentary into a single, unforgettable figure. The rat, at once the most humble and the most enduring of the artist's stencilled protagonists, recurs throughout his practice as an allegorical device through which to interrogate the failings of contemporary society. Reviled and relentlessly pursued, the rat's outcast status makes it an ideal emissary for Banksy's message. As the artist himself observed, "they exist without permission. They are hated, hunted, and persecuted. [...] And yet they are capable of bringing entire civilisations to their knees" (the artist in Banksy: Wall and Piece, London, 2005, p. 83).

The motif of Gangsta Rat features in several of the artist's most celebrated murals, realized in London at Farringdon in 2004 and at Old Street in 2006, and again in New York in 2013. The rat may be read as an alter ego for Banksy himself: a creature of the margins, most active under cover of darkness and adept at evading detection, yet ever present within the fabric of everyday urban life. Here, as elsewhere in his works, the autobiographical undertone is unmistakable. The rat becomes a proxy for the anonymous crusader who works by night in the service of equality and social justice.

The present work distills the urban and youth culture of the 1990s into a single, economical tableau. Rendered in the guise of a street-wise protagonist, the anthropomorphic rat sports a chain necklace and a baseball cap tilted at an angle, one paw resting nonchalantly upon a blaring boombox. The spray-painted tag above the stencilled figure sets the loose freedom of the hand against the precise containment of the template, a tension inherent to the execution of street art. This duality resonates throughout Banksy's career, which has been defined by a sustained exploration of the dialogue between spontaneous intervention and controlled reproduction.

Banksy has left an indelible mark upon the history of art, emerging as a true maverick of the genre. His bold, instantly recognizable stencils marry an acute sensitivity to current affairs with ideas of lasting resonance, a combination that has carried him from outsider street artist to one of the most significant and admired political and cultural voices of the twenty-first century. Executed in 2004, Gangsta Rat stands at the very heart of the mythology that surrounds Banksy's career and the cult following it has inspired.

description_block:
PROPERTY OF A LADY OF TITLEAHMED MATER (B. 1979)
Metropolis (from Desert of Pharan) 
mural-sized inkjet print
88 x 118 in (223.5 x 299.7 cm)
Executed in 2013, this work is one of two Artist's Proofs set aside from an edition of three

Provenance
Acquired directly from the artist by the present owner.

Exhibited
New York, The Brooklyn Museum, Ahmed Mater: Mecca Journeys, December 1, 2017 - June 17, 2018.

Literature
A. Mater, C. David, ed., Desert of Pharan: Unofficial Histories Behind the Mass Expansion of Mecca, Zürich, 2016 (illustrated pp. 113-14).

Ahmed Mater's monumental project Desert of Pharan includes hundreds of photographs, films, and documents that capture the rapid development of Mecca, Islam's holiest city, located in the western region of Saudi Arabia. The title refers to the ancient name for Mecca and the surrounding land, which is in a constant state of transformation and expansion in order to accommodate the tens of millions of pilgrims who journey there each year.

In the book Desert of Pharan: Unofficial Histories behind the Mass Expansion of Mecca (2016), Mater explains the origin of his project: "In 2008 I started a series of deliberately experimental journeys across, around, and within Mecca. Befriending immigrant workers on the Al Shamia building site (the site of the expansion of the Grand Mosque) led me to reflect on the combined histories and rapidly disintegrating and lost narratives of Mecca and its people – not only in relation to the communities who had once lived there but also the wider, global community of people who over the centuries had made the pilgrimage to this most visited yet most exclusive of sites." (p. 11)

In Mater's dramatic, massive aerial photograph Metropolis, Masjid al-Haram (the Grand Mosque) dominates the center of the composition. Its structure has evolved over the past 1,400 years and now stands as the largest mosque complex in the world. Begun in 2011/2012 by King Abdullah, the third Saudi expansion of the Grand Mosque added a massive northern annex, expanded the Mataaf (circumambulation courtyard), and interspersed bridges, tunnels, and service areas to improve circulation of the 1.85 million worshippers that it can accommodate at any one time. Behind the mosque stands the Makkah Royal Clock Tower, which measures 601 meters (1,972 feet) tall and features the world's largest clock face at 43 meters (141 feet) in diameter. It is the central and tallest building of the Abraj Al-Bait complex that houses multiple luxury hotels, a shopping mall, prayer halls, and many other amenities.

The present work captures the city's radiating design, with the Grand Mosque as the hub, supporting structures around it, and the dense sprawl of infrastructure stretching out toward the mountains. This birds' eye view offers a dizzying perspective of Mecca. Mater's hyper-clear photograph allows one to see individual people inside the Grand Mosque, streams of cars on the roadways, and the rigging on individual construction cranes, amidst many other details.

Metropolis functions as a seminal image within the Desert of Pharan series. This mural-sized photograph visualizes the physical realities of Mecca as well as underscores the social, cultural, economic, and environmental complexities of this sacred location. Summarizing Mecca's dramatic history and always-evolving state, Mater has written: "Mecca is being given a makeover, and the speed and breadth of its transformation is generating interrelated concerns regarding the city's social mechanics and the ongoing and symbolic relationship between demolition and construction." (p. 11)

Mater's mural-sized photographs from Desert of Pharan rarely appear at auction. Bonhams New York is honored to offer the present work.

Evening's Peace

Bob Ross Wet-on-Wet TechniqueÂ® on canvas

Painted in 1990

The proceeds from the sale of this lot will benefit American Public Television.

Bob Ross completed the present work for Volume 19 of his The Joy of Painting instructional book as Painting Twelve. Evening's Peace was the twelfth project out of thirteen in the volume. Once the printer returned the painting to Bob Ross Company, it was placed in secure storage, where it has remained since.

Bob took particular pride in the paintings that would be printed in his books; he knew that people would be studying the pages for years to come and would therefore spend as many as 3-5 hours on each "book" work.
